source_refs.note: Topic 1.7.5, printed page 12, as printed: the trends in electron affinity, Table 1.1 and Quick Check 1.7.

blocks.text: As the atomic size increases down the group, the larger electron cloud causes the incoming electron to experience less attraction from the nucleus. Consequently, electron affinity generally decreases down the group. This trend is observed in the halogens (At < I < Br < F < Cl). Generally, electron affinities become more negative as we move from left to right period. This is firstly due to increase in the nuclear charge, which attracts additional electrons more strongly and secondly due to decreasing atomic radius.

blocks.text: Explain with reasoning following facts about electron affinity:
bold: Explain with reasoning following facts about electron affinity:

blocks.prompt: a) 1st electron affinity of Oxygen is -141KJ/mol but 2nd electron affinity is +844.0 KJ/mol.
blocks.explanation: The first electron goes into a neutral oxygen atom; the nucleus attracts it and energy is released, so the value is negative. The second electron has to be added to the O⁻ ion, which is already negative and repels it; energy must be supplied to overcome this repulsion, so the value is positive (+798 kJ mol⁻¹ by the book's own data in 1.7.4; see the Book correction).

blocks.prompt: b) Which of nitrogen and phosphorus has the higher electron affinity? Justify with reason.
blocks.explanation: Phosphorus. Both have half-filled p subshells, but the 2p subshell of nitrogen is very small and compact, so an incoming electron meets more repulsion from the electrons already there. The 3p subshell of phosphorus is larger, so the new electron is repelled less and the electron affinity is higher (that of nitrogen is close to zero).

blocks.prompt: c) F has lower electron affinity than Cl although its size is smaller. Explain why?
blocks.explanation: A smaller size usually means stronger attraction, but the 2p subshell of fluorine is so small that its seven electrons strongly repel the incoming electron, and this repulsion offsets the attraction. The larger 3p subshell of chlorine has more room, so chlorine releases more energy (−349 against −328 kJ/mol).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book’s own text and equation in topic 1.7.4 give the second electron affinity of oxygen as +798 kJ mol⁻¹ (net +657 kJ mol⁻¹ for O²⁻), but this question prints +844.0. Data tables quote different values (about +798 and +844), so use the book’s +798 for consistency. The point of the question is the same: the second electron affinity is positive.
